paper_title: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-page document vision-language models encode each page independently, creating a feature-level discontinuity at page boundaries: visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages, and the language model must reason over these page representations formed in isolation. We introduce DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), a lightweight module inserted between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that injects the inductive bias of local cross-page context into visual representations. For each page, DocSEAM forms a local triplet with its two neighbors, applies center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates to fuse information from neighbor pages, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the visual token count unchanged. After a supervised cross-page warm-up and multi-page fine-tuning with DocSEAM frozen, our 9B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks. We further show that under controlled re-pagination, DocSEAM reduces sensitivity to boundary placement and improves cross-page span localization

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Multi-page document vision-language models (VLMs) (Bai et al., 2025b;a; Team, 2026; Zhu et al., 2025) typically encode each page independently and concatenate the resulting visual tokens into single sequence for the language model. This design is convenient and scalable, but it imposes an implicit assumption: the representation of page can be fully determined without seeing its neighbors. In practice, this assumption is routinely violated. Paragraphs continue across page breaks, tables carry rows onto the next page, and section headings introduce content that begins on the following leaf. When visual encoder commits to representation of the last row of table before seeing its continuation on the next page, the language model inherits feature-level discontinuity that it must repair from already-formed tokens. Can the language model repair this discontinuity on its own? In many cases, yes: the LLM can attend across pages, compare redundant evidence, and compensate for missing context. But we show empirically that this compensation is fragile. As shown in Fig. 1, when we re-paginate the same documents so that page breaks fall inside tables and paragraphs rather than between them, page-wise VLMs suffer consistent performance drop, even though the semantic content is unchanged (More analysis in Section 4.3). This pagination sensitivity suggests that independently formed visual representations may contribute to the models difficulty with cross-page reasoning: the language model must integrate information from page representations that were formed without access to neighboring pages. We address this with simple inductive bias: pages visual representation should be informed by its immediate neighbors before reaching the language model. We propose DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), lightweight module inserted between pretrained VLMs vision encoder and its language model. The module adds 235M parameters (2.6% of 9B backbone), does not modify the vision encoder or change the visual token budget, and is initialized as no-op so that training starts from the pretrained models known-good operating point. Two design choices encode document-specific structure. First, center-anchored attention mask allows the center page to attend to both neighbors while blocking direct interaction between the previous and next pages; this forces all cross-page information to flow through the center page, preventing two-hop leakage between non-adjacent pages within single layer. Second, directional salience gates, consisting of four learnable gates per token, modulate every cross-page attention cell, allowing the model to learn where cross-page communication is useful. In representative cross-page localization example, attention with DocSEAM concentrates on boundary-spanning evidence at an earlier LLM layer than with the baseline (Section 4.2). Our quantitative evaluation also shows improved cross-page span localization accuracy, indicating that DocSEAM helps the model identify evidence across page boundaries (Section 4.2). Our contributions are threefold: First, we identify pagination sensitivity as symptom in conventional document VLMs and design controlled re-pagination diagnostic to measure it. Second, we propose DocSEAM, simple post-encoder module that introduces the inductive bias of local crosspage context into multi-page document representations via center-anchored attention and directional salience gates. Third, we design an effective two-stage training strategy in which DocSEAM is first warmed up on supervised cross-page alignment tasks and then frozen during downstream finetuning, allowing the learned cross-page prior to transfer seamlessly across diverse tasks. Together, these contributions enable DocSEAM to achieve state-of-the-art performance across five representative multi-page document VQA benchmarks  (Fig. 1)  among end-to-end open-weight VLMs with fewer than 10B parameters, practically relevant model scale for document understanding.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Multi-page Document Visual Question Answering. Document VQA was originally posed as single-page problem (Mathew et al., 2021). Subsequent benchmarks extended it to multi-page settings: MP-DocVQA (Tito et al., 2023), DUDE (Van Landeghem et al., 2023). Current approaches fall into three families. Retrieval-augmented methods such as VisRAG (Yu et al., 2025), SV-RAG (Chen et al., 2025) and VDocRAG (Tanaka et al., 2025) select relevant pages before reading them, but still encode each page independently. Agentic methods like MACT (Yu et al., 2026) decompose reasoning into multi-step workflows (analysis, localization, reasoning) or multi-agent

For each page p, DocSEAM forms local triplet (Zp1, Zp, Zp+1), applies center-anchored self-attention with directional salience gates, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens Ep. The language model receives the same number of visual tokens as in the stateless baseline. pipelines, yet the per-page visual representation is never modified. End-to-end methods such as GRAM (Blau et al., 2024), DocSeeker (Yan et al., 2026), mPLUG-DocOwl2 (Hu et al., 2025), URaG (Shi et al., 2026), and Leopard (Jia et al., 2025) compress or reallocate visual tokens but still treat each page as an independently-encoded unit. Across all three families, visual token near page break is computed as if the page were self-contained; whatever cross-page reasoning happens, it happens after that representational commitment. DocSEAM modifies the page representation before it reaches the language model, retriever, or agent, and does so densely (every token) and directionally (tied to the specific neighbor). Visual Encoders for Documents. parallel line of work improves how single page is converted into visual tokens. Native-resolution ViTs (Dehghani et al., 2023) avoid aspect-ratio distortion on dense text; DAVE (Huang et al., 2026) pretrains an encoder specifically for documents and web UIs; DeepEncoder V2 (Wei et al., 2026) learns intra-page reading order via causal queries; UNIT (Zhu et al., 2024) unifies image and text recognition within one vision encoder and mPLUG-DocOwl2s H-Reducer compresses tokens while preserving layout. All of these improve intra-page representation quality. DocSEAM is complementary: it sits after whatever per-page encoder produced the token grid and opens channel between grids that were previously computed in isolation. Stateful and Multi-image Encoding. Most multi-image VLMs (Jiang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; 2025) use late fusion: images are encoded independently and cross-image reasoning is deferred to the LLM. Streaming VLMs propagate visual memory forward (Wang et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), but this memory is causal and mainly targets temporal compression. SVE (Wang et al., 2026) is the closest architectural prior: it injects causal cross-image interaction inside the ViT stack so the current image can condition on previous image. DocSEAM is complementary rather than direct variant. It leaves the vision encoder unchanged, operates post-encoder on the token grid consumed by the LLM, and uses bidirectional three-page neighborhood because documents are fully observed at inference. Its gates are also document-specific, learning which boundary tokens should send or receive cross-page context while suppressing margins, headers, and page numbers. Appendix compares SVE and DocSEAM under document fine-tuning.

sections.content: Let document consist of page images {I1, . . . , IP }. pretrained VLM vision encoder produces one visual-token sequence per page: Zp RNpd, (1) where Np is the number of visual tokens for page and is the hidden dimension consumed by the language model. With native-resolution preprocessing, Np depends on the page resolution and aspect ratio after resizing and merging, and can therefore vary across pages. In the standard multipage pipeline, the sequences Z1, . . . , ZP are concatenated and fed directly into the language model. Each pages representation is formed in complete isolation: the visual tokens at the bottom of page are produced without access to any pixel on page p+1, and vice versa. DocSEAM replaces each Zp with an enriched sequence of the same shape: Ep = DocSEAM(Zp1, Zp, Zp+1) RNpd. (2) The final visual-token sequence is [E1; . . . ; EP ], so the language model receives exactly the same number of visual tokens as in the baseline. DocSEAM is inserted after the vision encoder and before the language models multimodal input assembly. This placement has three practical advantages: it avoids modifying the pretrained vision tower, operates directly on the features the language model will consume, and makes the DocSEAM / no-DocSEAM comparison single-site architectural difference. 3.1 DOCUMENT-LOCAL TRIPLETS As shown in Fig. 2, for each page p, DocSEAM forms local triplet by concatenating the token grids of the previous, current, and next page: Xp = [ Zp1; Zp; Zp+1 ] R(Np1+Np+Np+1)d. (3) At document boundaries we use self-fallback, where Z0 = Z1, and ZP +1 = ZP , keeping the computation shape uniform without introducing learned null-page embedding. Each DocSEAM layer then applies masked self-attention over the triplet with two additive terms that control cross-page information flow: Attn(Q, K, ) = softmax (cid:18) QK dh (cid:19) + + V, (4) where is center-anchored triplet mask that determines which page groups may attend to each other (Section 3.2), and is directional salience bias that modulates how strongly individual tokens participate in cross-page attention (Section 3.3). Tokens from all three pages act as queries, keys, and values, but center-anchored mask  (Fig. 2)  restricts which page groups may communicate. The two neighbor pages are separated by two page transitions; they should exchange information only through the center-page representation. With stacked layers, the center page can still integrate information from neighbor states that interacted with it in earlier layers. The frontier term aligns directional send/receive gates with the corresponding ink boundaries, the margin term suppresses activations over whitespace, and Lbudget = max(0, ρ)2 penalizes mean gate activation above ρ = 0.20. Cross-entropy supplies the task-level supervision; further details are in Appendix B. Self-supervised boundary reconstruction was discarded as it led to gate collapse: global self-attention within each page allows masked tokens to be reconstructed without cross-page context (Appendix I). Stage B: Multi-page Document Fine-tuning. In Stage B, DocSEAM is frozen and the rest of the model is fine-tuned with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) on mixture of multi-page document understanding tasks. Freezing DocSEAM preserves its parameters learned in Stage while the downstream model adapts to the enriched tokens. The stateless baseline uses the same training-data pool and LoRA configuration, with Stage and Stage data combined in one SFT stage; training-strategy controls are reported in Section 4.4. Full dataset composition and hyperparameters for both stages are provided in Appendix A. Inference. At inference, each page is encoded once by the vision tower. DocSEAM processes the page triplets in single sliding-window pass, producing enriched tokens at no increase in the visual sequence length seen by the language model. Because the enrichment depends only on document pages, the enriched tokens can be computed once and reused across multiple questions about the same document. The additional inference cost of DocSEAM is small: two transformer layers over triplets of post-merger tokens, amounting to less than 7% of the total forward-pass FLOPs for typical 20-page document.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Backbone. We instantiate DocSEAM on Qwen3.5-9B (Team, 2026), native-resolution VLM with NaViT-style vision tower and 22 pixel-shuffle merger. DocSEAM adds L=2 transformer layers (235M parameters) between the Vision Encoder and the 9B language model. To demonstrate generality, we also report results with Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma3-4B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbones. Benchmarks. We evaluate on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks: DUDE (Van Landeghem et al., 2023), MP-DocVQA (Tito et al., 2023), SlideVQA (Tanaka et al., 2023), MMLongBench-Doc (Ma et al., 2024), and LongDocURL (Deng et al., 2025). DUDE and MPDocVQA use ANLS, while SlideVQA, MMLongBench-Doc, and LongDocURL use accuracy. We also report cross-page parsing results on MPDocBench-Parse (Zhou et al., 2026). Dataset details and task characteristics are provided in Appendix C. Baselines. Our primary comparison is matched stateless baseline: the same Qwen3.5-9B backbone, the same LoRA configuration, trained on the combined Stage and Stage data in single SFT stage. We show in Section 4.4 that adding Stage data to the baseline yields negligible change, so this setup is strictly more favorable to the baseline than using Stage data alone. We additionally compare against other multi-page document understanding methods. 4.1 MAIN RESULTS We compare DocSEAM against the proprietary models GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024) and Gemini 3 Pro (Google, 2026), as well as open-weight methods M3DocRAG (Cho et al., 2024), DocOwl2 (Hu et al., 2025), Vis-RAG (Yu et al., 2025), SV-RAG (Chen et al., 2025), VDocRAG (Tanaka et al., 2025), Docopilot (Duan et al., 2025), InternVL3 (Zhu et al., 2025), DocSeeker (Yan et al., 2026), and URaG (Shi et al., 2026). We also include the zero-shot Qwen3.5 (Team, 2026) backbone and its matched SFT baseline. Table 1 presents the main results. DocSEAM + Qwen3.5-9B achieves the best performance among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on all five benchmarks: 63.0 ANLS on DUDE (+5.4 over URaG), 89.2 ANLS on MP-DocVQA (+1.0 over URaG), 87.1 accuracy on SlideVQA (+10.0 over DocSeeker), 58.3 accuracy on MMLongBench-Doc (surpassing even Qwen3.5 zero-shot and all other open-weight models), and 62.9 accuracy on LongDocURL (+10.7 over URaG).

sections.title: 4.4 ABLATION STUDIES
sections.content: Table 4 presents key ablations on the two benchmarks most sensitive to cross-page reasoning. Capacity controls: the self-as-neighbor variant uses the identical DocSEAM architecture and FLOPs but feeds copies of the center page instead of real neighbors; its small gain (+0.6 on MMLongBench) supports the role of real neighboring-page context beyond added capacity. Two further controls match DocSEAMs parameter count without cross-page information: duplicating the last layers of the vision encoder and adding single-page transformer layers; both show similarly small gains (Appendix F). Bidirectional vs. causal: restricting to previous-page-only window degrades performance, validating that documents benefit from seeing both neighbors. Data attribution: to ensure gains are architectural rather than data-driven, our SFT baseline is trained on the combined Stage and Stage data in single stage; adding Stage data yields negligible change over Stage B-only SFT (44.5 vs. 44.3 on MMLongBench), suggesting that adding cross-page parsing data to standard SFT alone is insufficient to reproduce DocSEAMs gains. Training strategy: applying the twostage schedule to the stateless baseline reduces performance (42.1 vs. 44.5 on MMLongBench). To isolate the boundary curriculum from dedicated module adaptation, we instead train DocSEAM in Stage on the downstream mixture, keeping the same steps, batch size, CE and auxiliary losses, and Stage procedure. This control reaches 53.9 / 57.6, compared with 52.7 / 56.1 without Stage and 58.3 / 62.9 with boundary-focused Stage A. The additional +4.4 / +5.3 points support the boundary curriculum beyond providing an adaptation stage. Self-supervised boundary reconstruction also reduces performance (Appendix F). Full ablations including gate input variants, number of DocSEAM layers, and backbone generality are in Appendix F.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We identified pagination sensitivity as weakness of page-wise document VLMs and proposed DocSEAM, lightweight post-encoder module that enriches each pages visual tokens with bidirectional neighbor context through center-anchored attention and directional salience gates, without modifying the vision encoder or increasing the visual token budget. DocSEAM achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models (10B) on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks, improves cross-page span localization by 20.8 points over the SFT baseline, and reduces the pagination penalty to 0.8 and 0.7 points on MMLongBench-Doc and LongDocURL, respectively. Ablations suggest that neighboring-page context contributes to the gains beyond added capacity, while gate analysis shows directional specialization near content boundaries. These results highlight the value of incorporating local page continuity into document representations.

(4) Single-page lookup control (6k): the model localizes page-local evidence inside multi-page context. All examples are presented as document-local page neighborhoods. Stage hyperparameters. sections.title: B GATE AND LOSS DETAILS
sections.content: Content-frontier positional encoding. The positional feature ϕi R18 encodes each tokens distance to the top and bottom content frontiers (first and last rows containing document ink). The distance to each frontier is capped at fraction α = 0.20 of the page height and mapped via 4-frequency sinusoidal expansion: ψ(d) = (cid:2)d, sin(πd), cos(πd), . . . , sin(8πd), cos(8πd)(cid:3) R9, (12) yielding ϕi = [ψ(dtop(ri)); ψ(dbot(ri))]. Physical page edges often contain semantically irrelevant white space; measuring distance relative to detected ink frontiers rather than raw margins provides the gate with geometric prior invariant to blank page margins. Auxiliary gate loss. The gate alignment loss consists of three terms: Lgate = Lfrontier + λmarginLmargin + Lbudget, where Lfrontier applies weighted binary cross-entropy to align directional send/receive channels with content frontiers, Lmargin suppresses gate leakage over whitespace margins, and Lbudget = max(0, ρ)2 penalizes mean gate activation above the target budget ρ = 0.20. (13)

sections.title: C BENCHMARK DETAILS
sections.content: Document VQA benchmarks. We evaluate on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks that cover complementary document types and reasoning regimes. DUDE (Van Landeghem et al., 2023) is built from multi-industry, multi-domain, multi-page visually rich documents and includes diverse question and answer types, including layout-navigating and multi-step reasoning questions. We report ANLS following the benchmark protocol. MP-DocVQA (Tito et al., 2023) extends single-page document VQA to multi-page scanned industry documents by providing each question with its surrounding document pages, up to 20 pages per document. We report ANLS. SlideVQA (Tanaka et al., 2023) evaluates question answering over slide decks, where the model must identify relevant evidence slides and answer the question. We report exact-match accuracy. MMLongBench-Doc (Ma et al., 2024) targets long-context document understanding over lengthy PDF documents with evidence drawn from text, tables, charts, images, and layout structure. It includes both single-page and cross-page questions, as well as unanswerable questions for hallucination evaluation. We report accuracy. LongDocURL (Deng et al., 2025) evaluates long multimodal document understanding through tasks covering document understanding, numerical reasoning, and cross-element locating. We report accuracy.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Parsing benchmark. Beyond VQA, we evaluate on MPDocBench-Parse (Zhou et al., 2026), multi-page document parsing benchmark designed for document-level end-to-end parsing. Its evaluation protocol covers content fidelity and logical structure, including text, table, and formula recognition, truncated text and table merging, figure extraction, reading order, and heading hierarchy recovery. Because DocSEAM is designed to improve cross-page continuity, we focus on the two metrics most directly tied to page-boundary reasoning: truncated text merging and truncated table merging.

sections.title: H AGGREGATE GATE ACTIVATION STATISTICS
sections.content: The qualitative gate visualizations in Section 4.2 (Figure 4) show that DocSEAMs directional gates concentrate on boundary content and suppress blank margins. To verify that this behavior is systematic rather than cherry-picked, we compute aggregate gate activation statistics over 200 randomly sampled triplets from the MMLongBench-Doc benchmark.

We further divide each page into top band (top 20% of rows), bottom band (bottom 20%), and middle region. Content vs. margin selectivity. Across all gates and pages, mean activation on content regions is 0.27 vs. 0.19 on margins (1.4 ratio, Pearson ρ = 0.25 with the ink mask). While this ratio is moderate, the gates are not designed to be binary content detectors; their primary role is to directionally modulate cross-page attention flow, which the next analysis reveals. Directional boundary specialization. K.1 QUANTITATIVE COLUMN-ASYMMETRY ANALYSIS ON TWO-COLUMN DOCUMENTS The qualitative observations above suggest that DocSEAMs gates respect two-column layout structure. To verify this quantitatively, we measure the directional asymmetry of gate activation across left and right columns. In standard two-column document, the reading order flows from the left column to the right column on each page, then continues to the left column of the next page. Consequently, the continuation-relevant column differs by gate direction: gates mediating interaction with the next page (send to next, recv from next) should concentrate on the right column (where text exits the page), while gates mediating interaction with the previous page (recv from prev, send to prev) should concentrate on the left column (where text enters from the preceding page). Per-triplet column asymmetry. We extract gate activations for all 11 consecutive-page triplets of the same 13-page two-column scientific paper we showed earlier and split each gate heatmap into left and right halves (excluding 5% center gutter). Figure 9 shows the per-triplet comparison: across all four gates, the continuation-relevant column shows higher mean activation in 10 out of 11 triplets (91%). Quadrant-level analysis. To further localize the activation pattern, we divide each page into four quadrants (left-top, left-bottom, right-top, right-bottom using 30% boundary band) and average across all triplets. Figure 10 shows the result. The continuation-relevant corner activates 3.0 to 3.8 more than the diagonally opposite corner: send to next concentrates on right-bottom (0.347 vs. 0.096 at left-top, 3.6); recv from prev on left-top (0.383 vs. 0.123 at right-bottom, 3.1); recv from next on right-bottom (0.349 vs. 0.115 at left-top, 3.0); send to prev on left-top (0.372 vs. 0.098 at right-bottom, 3.8). This pattern matches the expected two-column reading order: text exits page from the right-column bottom and enters the next page at the left-column top. Multi-document validation. sections.title: L QUALITATIVE ANSWER COMPARISONS
sections.content: To visually inspect how DocSEAM improves multi-page document reasoning over baseline models, we examine representative qualitative examples where answering the question requires integrating information across adjacent pages. Figures 11 and 12 present side-by-side comparisons of predictions from DocSEAM, the matched baseline, and URaG, alongside ground-truth annotations and document evidence. Case 1: Cross-Page & Cross-Modal Evidence Integration (Figure 11). In this example from multi-page health report, the question asks which demographic group accounts for the largest proportion of high-cost health care users. The relevant text appears on Page 13, while supporting chart is located on Page 14. DocSEAM predicts the correct demographic group (60 and over age group) and grounds its explanation with page references. In contrast, the stateless baseline cites incorrect pages (Page 9 and Page 10 instead of Page 13 and Page 14) and lists multiple risk groups; these outputs alone do not identify the internal cause of the error. URaG outputs brief fragment (Individuals with chronic diseases) without citing evidence. Case 2: Structural Tracking Across Section Boundaries (Figure 12). This example evaluates structural section tracking over document page breaks. The prompt asks for the title of the section following Section 6 (Emergency Response). Section 6 concludes at the bottom of Page 50, and Section 7 begins at the top of Page 51. DocSEAM retrieves the complete section title (7 How do you recover and rehabilitate your property after disaster?). Conversely, the baseline model only produces generic label (Section 7), and URaG returns only single word (Recovery), missing the complete heading required by the ground truth.
